analysis.one_liner: Requires all new guns to carry a microscopic serial code on fired casings and a national ballistics database.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee with no cosponsors and no vote in the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every firearm made in or imported into the United States to be "microstamped" — a code etched inside the gun that imprints the gun's identifying characters onto every cartridge case it fires. It would also have required the Justice Department to run ballistics tests on crime guns in federal custody and build an electronic database that state and local police could search to link spent casings at crime scenes to specific guns.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people living with gun violence, whose communities would gain a tool for tracing shell casings at crime scenes back to the specific firearm and its last legal owner. Police and prosecutors investigating shootings would also benefit from searchable ballistics records across jurisdictions.

how_it_helps.text: Every new firearm must carry an etched array of characters identifying its make, model, and serial number, which transfers onto every cartridge case the gun fires, letting investigators match shell casings found at crime scenes to a specific gun.
The Attorney General would have to run ballistics tests on any firearm in federal custody believed involved in a federal or state crime and create an electronic database of the results.
The Attorney General would have to build a computer system through which state and local law enforcement agencies can promptly access the ballistics records, funded at $20 million per year.
An importer or manufacturer who makes or brings in a gun that is not microstamped, or whose microstamp fails to transfer to the casing, would lose their federal firearms license.

The Attorney General would have to report annually to the Judiciary Committees on how often ballistics records served as an investigative tool in investigations, arrests, indictments, and prosecutions, and how accessible the records are across jurisdictions.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers and importers, who would bear the cost of engraving microstamps on internal gun parts and of license revocation for noncompliant guns. The Treasury, through $20 million a year in appropriations for the ballistics database. Gun owners would face no direct cost, since the requirement applies at manufacture and import.

drawbacks.text: Microstamping technology was new in 2007, and gun makers argued in state debates on similar laws that the marks can be filed off or may not transfer reliably to casings — a cost and reliability objection an honest supporter would have to weigh.
The bill only covers newly manufactured or imported firearms, so it would take years for microstamped guns to make up a meaningful share of guns used in crimes, limiting near-term benefits.
It adds $20 million per year in federal spending for ballistics testing and the database, without clear evidence at introduction of how much that would improve case clearance rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a modest, targeted tool for solving gun crimes: shell casings are often left at shooting scenes, and readable identifying marks would let police trace them to a gun without a physical weapon. The costs fall narrowly on manufacturers and cost relatively little publicly. Its main weakness is scope — applying only to new guns means a slow pay-off — but the core mechanism serves a clear public-safety purpose with little burden on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime subcommittee until the Congress ended — no markup, no vote, and not a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews of New Jersey introduced the bill on April 17, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On June 25, 2007, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill never received a markup or floor vote and attracted no cosponsors before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers and importers, who avoided the cost of installing microstamping and the threat of license revocation, and nothing changed for police tracing of crime guns.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and took no further recorded action on it after its referral to subcommittee.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Crime subcommittee on June 25, 2007, and never reported it out or scheduled a markup.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed microstamping mandates as an unnecessary burden on firearms manufacturers and gun owners.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have forced every new gun to carry an etched identifying code on its internal parts, with license revocation for noncompliance — a manufacturing cost the industry did not want to bear. Because microstamping would have made it easier to trace guns used in crimes, the industry's interest in avoiding the requirement ran against the public's interest in solved shootings.
A $20 million annual authorization for ballistics testing and a shared electronic database would have expanded work and tools for crime labs and law enforcement agencies.
